867.t: The saucer on the coffin and benevolent societies
867.s: He has heard of putting a saucer on a laid-out man's chest for donations toward funeral costs but never saw it.
867.ch: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
867.q: Yeah, he would pay for whatever bill or his funeral, I guess, or something like that. You know, like a fellow don't have enough money to take care of his funeral and he finally had made a big debt for him or something like that. And they say, well, just put a saucer there. Well, that represents…

867.t: Neighbourhood collections to pay for a funeral band
867.s: Friends and neighbours pick up money to hire a band for a good-time guy's funeral, at a set band price.
867.ch: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
867.q: Oh, well, they pick up money, like I said, by the neighborhood. Just like it's a good time guy in this neighborhood, or a guy die, get killed, and he'd been a regular guy around the neighborhood. And he don't have enough money to have a band, see? Maybe the family can't. He's not able to pay for…

867.s: Brass band jobs like seeing off Kid Sheik or funerals for musicians are donated, while parades and most jobs are paid.
867.ch: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
867.q: It's a different kind of job. That's right. That's more of a donation. Like when they play, you know, send guys off or go meet guys like that. But I know that's more of a donation. If you want to go, you know, just donate your service like that. It's okay. Just like a lot of funerals we play. A lot…

14.t: Joining the Young Men's benevolent society
14.s: Love explains how burial societies worked, why musicians joined them to get funeral jobs for the Excelsior Band, and how he quit after a fight over an election.
14.q: Well that was a society, you know. You pay so much, let me see, was it every week? Every quarter, they'd have a meeting just like the union. I don't know, I believe it was a dollar a quarter or something like that. I can't remember exactly, but anyhow, when you die they bury you, you see. They give…

14.t: Getting funeral jobs by visiting sick society members
14.s: Love and Allen describe bandleaders such as Allen and Carnish who visited dying society members to line up the funeral job in advance.
14.q: Yeah. Allen used to, yeah, you know, one of them societies, and the men would get some jobs, and the men would get sick, you know, it'd be low, you know. Allen would go see him, you know, go visit him. And if he just thought that man wasn't going to live like that, you know, he'd say, well, tell…

138.t: Pay for funerals and earlier white and colored funeral bands
138.s: Funeral pay was three dollars a man; Laine recalls two colored brass bands and white bands such as Brookhoven's playing before him.
138.q: Yes, it was two colored bands that I remember. Two colored bands only. And brass bands, but I don't remember any orchestra. Remember nothing like that. And the man that had the first band was, oh, I can't speak of his name now. But anyhow, he had a military band and believe me, he had a pretty good…

138.t: Music at funerals and the Gretna and Algiers parks
138.s: Laine describes march music after the burial, the Lee Benevolent and Owls clubs, and regular park and racetrack jobs across the river.
138.q: Then the minister or priest or whatever... He had that taken. He's held a ceremony over his body. They mean a Christian. Right after that we'd march all out, we'd walk out, not march, walk out to the gate of the cemetery and the organizations would form up right there. Then we'd start from there.…

864.t: How brass bands get their jobs: organizations and friends
864.s: Brass band jobs come through organizations and personal contacts; Tillman tells how a Gonzales group tracked him down for the Young Tuxedo, and churches only hire for marches.
864.q: They get them through being members of organizations. They get them through friends that know them better than they know others. See if they, it's like if you have a friend, regardless of what he is, if you got something that you can do in his way, you give it to him. Now regardless of who he…

181.t: Cigar-box collections to hire a funeral band
181.s: Mac and Parker explain bands hired by passing the cigar box for a well-known man.
181.ch: Church funerals, band size and mourning
181.q: So-and-so, they had to eat, don't belong to nothing, give me a cigar box. This fella get one, that fella get one. Go around all the ballrooms, everywhere.

430.s: After a brief close of the sticks-arrest story, he explains that societies and clubs hired music for funerals, often several bands; Excelsior and the Onward were best, and undertakers now discourage music.
430.q: Not cool. Yeah, I was playing on this lady's step. And she said I used to know her, you see. So she had me arrested, see. So when I go to the judge, I could play the sticks pretty good, you know. So the judge said, well, can you play? I said, yeah, that's a good play so I played the job. And he…

646.t: Wakes, burial and burial societies on the plantation
646.s: Mrs. Cary describes burial the next day, singing at wakes, burial societies like Loving Charity, and summer picnics.
646.q: Yeah. They bury them the next day. The next day? They couldn't keep them like they do now. Yeah. After they die the day, they bury them the next day. Well, what would happen? They wake them one night. Would they sing at the wake? Ma'am. Would they sing when they were waking? Yeah. They sing. Oh,…

710.t: Burial societies, dues and music for funerals
710.s: Bailey explains how benevolent societies paid for funerals and music, the monthly and quarterly dues, and that members wore their own black clothes.
710.q: Yeah, yeah, because I was into myself with music. Yeah, I used to be in society with music. Plenty of funerals with music.

873.t: Benevolent societies, burials and unpaid band playing
873.s: The societies Benefisence, God Helpers and others bury members; bands played free, and only for musicians.
873.q: Well, if one of the members of the Benefisence members died, well, they better remember. What's the name of it? Benefisence, that's the French name. And then they have God Helpers. And they have, well, they have Ease Light. That was all the benevolent society.

839.t: Cigar box collections and music at burials
839.s: None of them knew of collecting money for a band at funerals; burials with music and stopping at the graveyard.
839.q: I was gonna ask you another thing. What about this cigar box deal you know like they take a collection for a guy when he dies? To hire a band. Did you ever play any of those? Yeah. Seagull box deal. I was gonna ask you another thing.

42.t: Parades, funerals, pay and the brass bands
42.s: He talks of parades, the rising number of funerals, pay of five or six dollars, a long Tuxedo funeral and the Gibson band.
42.ch: Playing in New Orleans and influences
42.q: and uh lachins no i've done pretty badly that way there's been uh i haven't done at all well that way i've never been out to happy landings oh these people always i've always had a transportation problem yeah i don't drive and by the time you can talk somebody into taking you you there they they…

628.t: Benefit jobs and a Zulu grand marshal's funeral
628.s: Williams tells of a good-hearted man at Sam's who died, a woman who collected three hundred dollars with a cigar box to hire the band, and a Zulu grand marshal buried with scrounged money.
628.q: He was riding in Ramport, that's where we used to pass him. A guy, he was a good, a good Samurit, he used to give a good play on the card game, the Pity Pat game at Sam's where they sell those uh, those Samurit's, poor boy Sam. So they thought they'd give him a big cent off because he was a good…

630.t: Burying with a band and passing the saucer
630.s: In earlier times people were buried with a band paid for by passing a saucer, now a cigar box.
630.q: Yep. Bury with a band of music like they do now. Sometimes two bands. Sometimes two bands. According to what the fellow brought. Then way back in them times, the fellow could die on the corner and get buried. He didn't have to worry about no insurance. If he bumped on the corner there, the man pick…

632.t: Who hired bands for private parties
632.s: Private parties and committees hired bands; the friends' own parties at Otto's treated the band as social guests.
632.q: Think People Would Sometimes If They Had An Organization The Committee Entertainment Committee Although Members Or Chairman Perhaps Would Make Arrangements For The Band More Specifically Than That I Can't Say

779.t: Playing funerals as a boy and the early union
779.s: Union bands at funerals in Gretna, political meetings, playing union and non-union as a youth.
779.q: Oh yeah, I played for funerals when I was real young over in Gretna. You see, years ago, the Musicians Union, now this wasn't for no musician, this one, or these D's that I played, but the musicians used to furnish a ten piece band when a member died, and the band used to play at the church. And…

405.s: Bull explains how brass bands began at Australian jazz conventions, older musicians' scorn, and the lack of friendly societies.
405.q: When did these brass bands start really? About three or four years ago I think was the first one at the convention. Of course you have all the old Aiden Monspras and all the old Lou Waters type musicians go, what's all this rubbish, what's this garbage, that's not jazz. Anyway, they started off…

127.t: Upcoming band gigs and Punch's pawned instrument
127.s: Allen mentions bands playing tomorrow and possible gigs; Punch says his instrument is in pawn.
127.q: your uncle has it my uncle has it I ain't been able to get it to him I keep the entrance up on it but I ain't been able to get it out I ain't given ten dollars on it and I can't get a clear

128.t: Benevolent societies, dues and funeral brass bands
128.s: The men explain how societies paid for funerals and brass bands through monthly dues.
128.q: Yeah, when you lose your members, your dead members, you'll be taxed. Some of them 50 cents. Now my daddy belongs to the Prosperity. Used to be that, you remember the old, Hall and Vera, Brother Hall's Church there. The old Vera between Boeben and St. Anthony. Preservative? That's where that would…

177.t: Societies, the union and funeral bands
177.s: Jiles explains how societies paid for bands, musicians once played for free, and how the union now handles funeral bands.
177.q: Well at that time the union wasn't in demand and every musician didn't belong to the union and it wasn't as particular. You could play with a band, a man wasn't in the union and nobody got farm or nothing. They hadn't gotten to that stage. I understand now the bands that you see, that gets by me if…

58.t: How often jump-up bands played funerals and who hired them
58.s: Miller says about four funerals a month, bands going out of town on weekends, Monday-night dances, and clubs and societies hiring leaders for funerals.
58.q: In the street? Oh, would that call it a funeral? Well, like in, like Labor Day, Mardi Gras, 4th of July, or somebody died, you know, we'll play a funeral.

890.t: Who paid the musicians for funerals
890.s: Questions about band leader contracts and whether the family of the deceased pays; the ritual was already old when he arrived.
890.ch: New Orleans funerals and early working life
890.q: Well I would state he had a contract, but someone gives him X amount of dollars to take care of the person that you are using. But I never had a job myself as the band leader to play a funeral.
